collection_intro: Hands-on labs for sections 9.1 to 9.13 of *Java Programming*, 10th edition. Each lab takes 20 to 30 minutes: read the code and predict what it does, fix or write it, check its structure, run the test program in your IDE and compare the output, then explain your choices. Lab 9.13 uses records, so use JDK 16 or later. Submit the lab report to Blackboard.

labs.title: The audiobook that never got the label fix
labs.subtitle: An AudioBook “is a” Book; a Library “has” books
objectives: Use the “is a” test to decide which class should inherit from which
Tell inheritance (is-a) apart from containment (has-a)
Explain how reusing a tested parent class reduces errors
labs.scenario:
The Eastside Branch library catalogs printed books with `Book` and audiobooks with `AudioBook`. Last year someone made `AudioBook` by copying every line of `Book.java` and adding a narrator. Last month the catalog label was fixed in `Book` to read *Title by Author*, but the copy in `AudioBook` still prints *Title - Author*, so the two kinds of item no longer match.

There is a second problem. To reuse `setTitle()` for the branch name, someone wrote `Library extends Book`. Now the compiler accepts nonsense such as asking a library for its author, and an audiobook can't even go on a `Book` shelf.

`Book.java` is tested and read-only. Make `AudioBook` inherit from it and remove the copied code, and give `Library` its own name instead of pretending to be a book. The test program then prints:

```
Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler
Kindred by Octavia E. Butler, narrated by Lena Okoro
Eastside Branch holds 2 items
Item 2 on the shelf: Kindred by Octavia E. Butler
```

requirements.text: `AudioBook` inherits from `Book` and declares only what is new: the `narrator` field and its two methods.
`Library` does not inherit from `Book`. It keeps the branch name in its own `private String` field, and still *has* books in its `Book[] shelf`.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

files.name: Book.java
AudioBook.java
Library.java

labs.solution_notes: An audiobook passes the “is a” test (an AudioBook is a Book, not the other way around), so `AudioBook` inherits every field and method of `Book` and only adds the narrator (pp. 330–331). Deleting the copy also deletes the stale `getLabel()`: the inherited version is the one that was fixed and tested, which is the “reduce errors” benefit on p. 330. A library fails the “is a” test (a library is not a book); it *has* books, which is containment (aggregation, because the books would still exist if the branch closed; p. 331). The `extends` keyword is explained in section 9.2; here it is enough to know it is how Java writes “inherits from”.

warmup.question: Say each pair in an “is a” sentence: AudioBook/Book and Library/Book. Which sentence is true?
warmup.model_answer: “An AudioBook is a Book” is true. “A Library is a Book” is false; a library has books.

warmup.question: With the starter, what would `branch.getLabel()` return for the Eastside Branch library, and why does the compiler allow the call at all?
warmup.model_answer: It would return “Eastside Branch by null”. Library extends Book, so it inherits getLabel() and the author field, even though a library has no author.

checks.title: AudioBook inherits from Book
checks.message: Write the header as `public class AudioBook extends Book`: an audiobook is a book, so it should receive Book's fields and methods instead of copying them.
checks.hint: Which keyword in the Library header already says “inherits from”?

checks.title: AudioBook keeps only what is new
checks.message: Delete the copied `title` and `author` fields, their get and set methods, and the old `getLabel()`. Keep `narrator` and its two methods. The inherited versions are the tested ones, including the fixed label.

checks.title: Library is not a Book
checks.message: Remove `extends Book` from the Library header. A library has books; it is not one, so it shouldn't inherit an author or a label.

checks.title: Library stores its own name
checks.message: Declare a field such as `private String name;` and set it in the constructor. Once Library no longer extends Book, `setTitle()` isn't available, and the name was never a title anyway.

checks.title: getName() returns that field
checks.message: Return the library's own name field from `getName()`, not `getTitle()`.

After `AudioBook extends Book`, every line that also appears in Book.java can go. What is left is the narrator.
In Library, replace `extends Book` with a String field of Library's own: set it in the constructor and return it from `getName()`.

test_program.how_to_run: Put `Book.java`, `AudioBook.java`, `Library.java` and `TestLibrary.java` in the same folder, then run `javac *.java` and `java TestLibrary`. In an IDE, add all of them to one project and run `TestLibrary.java`. You don't type anything: the test program supplies the data.

reflection.question: The label bug was fixed once, in Book, yet audiobooks kept the old label. Explain how inheritance would have prevented that.
reflection.model_answer: With inheritance there is only one getLabel(), the one in Book. Fixing it fixes every subclass at once; a copied method has to be found and fixed separately, and this copy was forgotten.

reflection.question: Why is `Library extends Book` worse than the duplicated code in AudioBook, even though it saved the programmer some typing?
reflection.model_answer: It claims a library is a book, so Library inherits an author, a label and setTitle() that make no sense for it, and the compiler can no longer catch misuse. Containment (a name field plus a Book array) models what a library really is.

labs.extension: Add a `PrintedBook` class with a `pages` field. Which class should it extend, and what is the only code it needs? Then write the “is a” and “has a” sentences for `Library`, `Book` and a new `Member` class that can borrow up to five books.
labs.worth_knowing: “Favor object composition over class inheritance” is one of the best-known rules in software design. It comes from the 1994 book *Design Patterns*, whose four authors are nicknamed the Gang of Four. Use `extends` only when the “is a” sentence is true.

labs.title: The VIP who was sent to the general line
labs.subtitle: A subclass adds what only it needs; instanceof asks what an object is
objectives: Use `extends` so a subclass receives its parent's fields and methods
Put a field and its methods in the most specific class that needs them
Use `instanceof` to test whether an object is a member of a class
labs.scenario:
The Harbor Hall concert venue sells general tickets and VIP tickets. A VIP ticket includes drink vouchers, but when vouchers were added they went into `Ticket`, so every general ticket carries a voucher count of 0 that means nothing.

Worse, the entrance scanner decides the lane by counting vouchers. On Saturday a VIP guest who had already used both vouchers rescanned at the door and was sent to the general line.

Move the vouchers into `VipTicket`, where they belong, and make `Gate.laneFor()` ask what kind of ticket it has been given, not how many vouchers are left. The test program then prints:

```
Seat F12, $45.0: General lane
Seat A3, $180.0, vouchers left 0: VIP lane
A VipTicket is a Ticket: true
A Ticket is a VipTicket: false
```

requirements.text: `Ticket` has no vouchers at all. `VipTicket` declares `private int vouchers` and the methods `getVouchers()`, `setVouchers(int)` and `useVoucher()`.
`Gate.laneFor()` sends a ticket to the VIP lane when it is a `VipTicket` (use `instanceof`), whatever its voucher count.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

files.name: Ticket.java
VipTicket.java
Gate.java

labs.solution_notes: `VipTicket extends Ticket`, so it already has a seat, a price and their get and set methods; it only adds what is particular to it, as `DinnerParty` adds `dinnerChoice` to `Party` (pp. 335–336). Inheritance is one-way: a parent can't use its child's members, and it shouldn't carry fields that only some children need (p. 333). `instanceof` is true when the object on the left is a member or descendant of the class on the right (p. 333), so `t instanceof VipTicket` is true for every VIP ticket, used vouchers or not. Once `Ticket` has no `getVouchers()`, the starter's `laneFor()` no longer compiles, which forces the change. Passing a `VipTicket` to a `Ticket` parameter works because every VipTicket is a Ticket; section 9.9 explains this in detail.

warmup.question: In the starter, a general ticket for seat F12 calls `getVouchers()`. What does it return, and does that number mean anything?
warmup.model_answer: It returns 0. The number means nothing, because general tickets never come with vouchers; the field shouldn't exist for them.

warmup.question: The starter's `laneFor()` tests `t.getVouchers() > 0`. Describe a VIP ticket for which this test gives the wrong lane.
warmup.model_answer: A VIP ticket whose vouchers have all been used (count 0), or one that was sold without vouchers. The test says General lane even though it is a VIP ticket.

checks.message: Remove the `vouchers` field and `getVouchers()`, `setVouchers()` and `useVoucher()` from Ticket. A general ticket has no vouchers, and a parent class shouldn't hold what only one child needs.

checks.title: VipTicket holds the vouchers
checks.message: Declare `private int vouchers;` in VipTicket. Don't redeclare the seat or the price: VipTicket inherits them from Ticket.

checks.title: VipTicket has the three voucher methods
checks.message: Move `getVouchers()`, `setVouchers(int)` and `useVoucher()` into VipTicket, with the same headers they had in Ticket.

checks.title: The gate checks the kind of ticket
checks.message: Test `t instanceof VipTicket`. Being a VIP depends on the kind of ticket, not on how many vouchers are left.
checks.hint: instanceof is written in lowercase, with the object on the left and the class on the right.

hints: Cut the field and its three methods from Ticket and paste them into VipTicket. Nothing else in Ticket changes.
After the move, `t.getVouchers()` no longer compiles in Gate: a plain Ticket has no such method. That's the line to replace.
The condition you need is an `instanceof` expression with `t` on the left and the VIP class on the right.

Seat F12, $45.0: General lane
Seat A3, $180.0, vouchers left 0: VIP lane
A VipTicket is a Ticket: true
A Ticket is a VipTicket: false
test_program.predict: Before you change anything, run the test program with the starter and predict the lane for seat A3: it was sold with 2 vouchers and `useVoucher()` is called three times. Then predict the last two lines: which way does `instanceof` work?
test_program.how_to_run: Put `Ticket.java`, `VipTicket.java`, `Gate.java` and `TestGate.java` in the same folder, then run `javac *.java` and `java TestGate`. In an IDE, add all of them to one project and run `TestGate.java`. You don't type anything: the test program supplies the data.

reflection.question: Why is `instanceof VipTicket` a better test than counting vouchers? Use seat A3 in your answer.
reflection.model_answer: Seat A3 is a VIP ticket whatever happens to its vouchers. instanceof asks what the object is, which never changes; the voucher count changes as the guest uses vouchers, so it can't identify a VIP.

reflection.question: `vip instanceof Ticket` is true but `general instanceof VipTicket` is false. Explain why in terms of “is a”.
reflection.model_answer: Every VipTicket is a Ticket because it extends Ticket, but a plain Ticket is not a VipTicket. Inheritance goes one way, from parent to child.

labs.extension: Add a `StudentTicket` subclass with a `schoolId` field. Without touching `Gate`, which lane does a student go to? Then add a third lane for students and decide where in `laneFor()` its `instanceof` test must go.
labs.worth_knowing: Since Java 16, `instanceof` can also name the object it just tested: `if (t instanceof VipTicket vip)` makes `vip` usable as a VipTicket inside the `if`, so you can call `vip.getVouchers()` right away. This is called pattern matching for instanceof.

labs.title: The day pass that costs $25.0 per month
labs.subtitle: Override with the same name and parameter list, and let @Override check it
objectives: Override a parent method by writing a child method with the same name and parameter list
Tell overriding apart from overloading
Use the `@Override` annotation so the compiler catches a method that doesn't override
labs.scenario:
Dock 9 Coworking prints a rate on every receipt with `rateLabel()`. The standard `Plan` is billed by the month. A `DayPass` was supposed to print *per day*, and its author wrote the method, but every day-pass receipt still says **$25.0 per month**. Nobody saw an error message.

The new `HourlyDesk` has the same problem in a different form: it has a `rateLabel(int hours)` for the booking screen, but the receipt calls `rateLabel()` with no arguments and gets the monthly wording.

`Plan.java` is read-only. Make both subclasses override `rateLabel()` properly, and mark each override with `@Override` so this can't happen silently again. The test program then prints:

```
Monthly: $250.0 per month
Day pass: $25.0 per day
Hot desk: $6.5 per hour
Hot desk, 4 hours: $26.0 for 4 hours
```

requirements.text: `DayPass` overrides `rateLabel()` (same name, same empty parameter list) and marks it `@Override`; its label ends in `per day`.
`HourlyDesk` keeps its `rateLabel(int hours)` and also overrides `rateLabel()`, marked `@Override`, with a label ending in `per hour`.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

files.name: Plan.java
DayPass.java
HourlyDesk.java

labs.solution_notes: A child method overrides a parent method only when both the name and the parameter list match; with a child object, the child's version then runs (p. 337). `ratelabel()` with a lowercase *l* is simply a new method, so `day.rateLabel()` runs the inherited `Plan` version. `rateLabel(int hours)` has a different parameter list, so it overloads the parent method and the object has both versions (p. 337). `@Override` asks the compiler to confirm the method overrides something; on `ratelabel()` it produces “method does not override or implement a method from a supertype” (pp. 337–339). Using one name, `rateLabel()`, for every kind of plan is subtype polymorphism (p. 337).

warmup.question: With the starter, which class's `rateLabel()` runs for `day.rateLabel()`, and why doesn't the DayPass method run?
warmup.model_answer: Plan's version runs. DayPass's method is named ratelabel with a lowercase l, so it is a different method that doesn't override rateLabel().

warmup.question: HourlyDesk has `rateLabel(int hours)`. Does it override `Plan.rateLabel()`? What happens when the receipt calls `desk.rateLabel()`?
warmup.model_answer: No. Its parameter list is different, so it overloads the method. desk.rateLabel() with no arguments runs Plan's version and prints per month.

checks.message: Name the method `rateLabel` exactly as in Plan (capital L, no parameters) and put `@Override` on the line above it. Java names are case-sensitive, so `ratelabel` is a different method.
checks.hint: Compare the DayPass header with the one in Plan.java letter by letter.

checks.title: HourlyDesk overrides rateLabel() too
checks.message: Add a second method, `@Override public String rateLabel()` with no parameters. Keep `rateLabel(int hours)`: the booking screen still uses that overload.

checks.title: The hot-desk label says per hour
checks.message: The no-argument label should be built like Plan's, ending in `" per hour"`, for example `"$" + getRate() + " per hour"`.

hints: Overriding needs two things to match the parent: the method name, letter for letter, and the parameter list.
`@Override` goes on the line just above the method header. Put it on `ratelabel()` first and read the compiler's message.
HourlyDesk ends up with two methods named `rateLabel`: one with an `int` parameter (overload) and one with none (override).

Monthly: $250.0 per month
Day pass: $25.0 per day
Hot desk: $6.5 per hour
Hot desk, 4 hours: $26.0 for 4 hours
test_program.predict: Before you change anything, predict all four lines the starter prints. Which of them will say per month?
test_program.how_to_run: Put `Plan.java`, `DayPass.java`, `HourlyDesk.java` and `TestPlans.java` in the same folder, then run `javac *.java` and `java TestPlans`. In an IDE, add all of them to one project and run `TestPlans.java`. You don't type anything: the test program supplies the data.

reflection.question: The starter compiled and ran without a single error, yet two receipts were wrong. How would `@Override` have changed that?
reflection.model_answer: With @Override on ratelabel(), the compiler would have refused it because it overrides nothing. The typo would have been caught at compile time instead of on customers' receipts.

reflection.question: HourlyDesk now has two methods named `rateLabel`. Explain which one runs for `desk.rateLabel()` and for `desk.rateLabel(4)`, and why both may exist.
reflection.model_answer: desk.rateLabel() runs the override with no parameters; desk.rateLabel(4) runs the overload with an int. Methods may share a name when their parameter lists differ, and Java picks one by the arguments.

labs.extension: Add a `MeetingRoom` plan billed per booking. Write its override first *without* `@Override` and with a deliberate typo, run the test, then add `@Override` and read the compiler message. Which version would you rather discover in production?
labs.worth_knowing: Annotations such as `@Override` arrived in Java 5, in 2004. Before that, a misspelled override compiled silently, exactly like `ratelabel()`. Other languages added the same safety net later: C# requires the `override` keyword, and Python 3.12 added an `@override` decorator for type checkers.

labs.title: The hotel suites that won't compile
labs.subtitle: When the parent needs arguments, the child's constructor must call super() first
objectives: Predict the order in which parent and child constructors run
Call a parent constructor that requires arguments with `super(...)` as the first statement
Write a child constructor that passes a constant to its parent
labs.scenario:
The Seawall Hotel registers every room with `Room`, whose only constructor requires a room number and a nightly rate. A developer added `Suite` and `StaffRoom`, and the build broke: the compiler reports that `Room` can't be constructed without arguments.

Suites need their number and rate passed on to `Room`, plus a bedroom count of their own. Staff rooms are never rented, so the front desk only ever gives a number; their rate is always $0.0.

`Room.java` is read-only. Write the constructors so each subclass gives `Room` what it needs. The test program then prints (notice which line comes first for the suite):

```
Room 101 registered at $129.0 a night
Room 501 registered at $349.0 a night
  Suite 501 has 2 bedrooms
Room B12 registered at $0.0 a night
Suite 501: $349.0, 2 bedrooms
Staff room B12: $0.0
```

requirements.text: `Suite`'s constructor passes the room number and rate to `Room` with `super(...)` as its first statement, then sets `bedrooms` itself.
`StaffRoom` has a constructor with one parameter, the room number, that calls `super(...)` with that number and a rate of `0.0`.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

files.name: Room.java
Suite.java
StaffRoom.java

labs.solution_notes: Creating a subclass object runs the superclass constructor first, then the subclass constructor (p. 339), which is why “Room 501 registered” prints before “Suite 501 has 2 bedrooms”. A constructor that doesn't call `super(...)` gets an automatic call to the parent's no-argument constructor; `Room` has none, so the starter fails to compile, like Figure 9-9 (p. 343). When a superclass has only constructors that require arguments, each subclass constructor must call one with `super(arguments)` as its first statement (pp. 340–341, Table 9-1). The child constructor need not match the parent's parameters: `StaffRoom(String)` passes a constant `0.0`, like the `HourlyEmployee()` example on p. 341. Java does not allow `Room(...)` by name; you must write `super`.

warmup.question: Read `Room.java`. Can you write `new Room()` with no arguments? Why does that matter for `Suite`?
warmup.model_answer: No: Room's only constructor requires a number and a rate, and writing it removed the automatic default constructor. Suite's constructor implicitly calls Room() unless told otherwise, so it fails to compile.

warmup.question: When `new Suite("501", 349.0, 2)` runs, which constructor's message prints first, Room's or Suite's?
warmup.model_answer: Room's. The superclass constructor always runs before the subclass constructor's own statements.

checks.message: Make `super(roomNumber, rate);` the very first statement of the Suite constructor, before setting `bedrooms`. Java doesn't let you call `Room(...)` by name; use `super`.
checks.hint: Only comments may come before super(...) in a constructor.

checks.title: StaffRoom passes a $0.0 rate to Room
checks.message: Write `public StaffRoom(String roomNumber)` whose first statement is `super(roomNumber, 0.0);`. The child constructor's parameters don't have to match the parent's; it only has to pass what Room needs.

hints: Compile the starter and read the first error: which constructor is Java looking for, and in which class?
In Suite, the parent's two values are already parameters: `roomNumber` and `rate`. Hand them to `super(...)`.
StaffRoom takes one parameter but Room needs two. The second one is a constant you know.

Room 501 registered at $349.0 a night
  Suite 501 has 2 bedrooms
Room B12 registered at $0.0 a night
Suite 501: $349.0, 2 bedrooms
Staff room B12: $0.0
test_program.predict: Before you fix anything, compile the starter and predict the error message. After the fix, predict how many lines `new Suite("501", 349.0, 2)` prints, and in what order.
test_program.how_to_run: Put `Room.java`, `Suite.java`, `StaffRoom.java` and `TestRooms.java` in the same folder, then run `javac *.java` and `java TestRooms`. In an IDE, add all of them to one project and run `TestRooms.java`. You don't type anything: the test program supplies the data.

reflection.question: Why must the Room part of a Suite be built before the Suite part? Use `getNumber()` in the Suite constructor as your example.
reflection.model_answer: The Suite constructor calls getNumber(), which reads Room's number field. That field only has a value once Room's constructor has run, so the parent must be built first.

reflection.question: StaffRoom's constructor has one parameter while Room's has two. Why is that allowed?
reflection.model_answer: A child constructor only has to call super(...) with the arguments the parent needs. It can supply them from its own parameters or from constants, so StaffRoom passes its number plus 0.0.

labs.extension: Give `Room` a second constructor `Room(String roomNumber)` that calls `this(roomNumber, 99.0)`. Now which subclass constructors still need `super(...)`, according to Table 9-1? Then try putting `bedrooms = numBedrooms;` above `super(...)` and read the error.
labs.worth_knowing: Every constructor chain ends at `Object`, the class every Java class descends from (section 9.11). So `new Suite(...)` runs three constructors: Object's, then Room's, then Suite's. If you write no `super(...)` at all, the compiler quietly inserts `super();` for you.

labs.title: The insured parcel that never finishes printing
labs.subtitle: Inside an override, super.method() runs the parent's version
objectives: Call an overridden parent method from the child with `super.methodName()`
Explain the difference between `label()`, `this.label()` and `super.label()` inside an override
Extend a parent's result instead of copying its formula
labs.scenario:
Gulf Courier prints a label and a price for every parcel. `InsuredShipment` overrides both methods so they include the insurance, and both overrides are broken.

- `totalCost()` copies the parent's formula from last winter, with the old rate of $4.0 per kg. Shipping went up to $4.5 in March, so every insured parcel is undercharged.
- `label()` was meant to reuse the parent's label, but printing the first insured label crashes the program with a `StackOverflowError`.

`Shipment.java` is read-only and its fields are private. Make both overrides build on the parent's version. The test program then prints:

```
Shipment #1001 to Miami, 2.0 kg
Total: $14.0
Shipment #1002 to Denver, 2.0 kg, insured for $500.0
Insurance fee: $10.0
Total: $24.0
```

requirements.text: `InsuredShipment.totalCost()` returns the parent's `totalCost()` plus `insuranceFee()`; it repeats no rates or formulas from Shipment.
`InsuredShipment.label()` returns the parent's `label()` followed by `, insured for $` and the insured value.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

files.name: Shipment.java
InsuredShipment.java

labs.solution_notes: When a child overrides a method but still needs the parent's version, it calls `super.methodName()` (p. 344), as `PreferredCustomer.display()` calls `super.display()` in Figure 9-11. Inside the override, plain `label()` and `this.label()` both mean the child's own version (p. 345), so the starter's `label()` calls itself again and again until the call stack runs out: a `StackOverflowError`. `super.totalCost()` reuses Shipment's current formula, so the March price change reaches insured parcels too. Unlike a `super(...)` constructor call, `super.method()` does not have to be the first statement (p. 344); here it is part of the `return` expression.

warmup.question: Inside `InsuredShipment.label()`, the starter calls `label()`. Which class's `label()` is that, and what happens next?
warmup.model_answer: It is InsuredShipment's own label(), the method that is running. It calls itself, which calls itself again, forever, until Java throws a StackOverflowError.

warmup.question: For a 2.0 kg parcel insured for $500.0, what does the starter's `totalCost()` return, and what should it return?
warmup.model_answer: The starter returns 5.0 + 8.0 + 10.0 = 23.0. It should return Shipment's 5.0 + 9.0 = 14.0 plus the 10.0 fee, which is 24.0.

checks.title: totalCost() builds on the parent's cost
checks.message: Return `super.totalCost() + insuranceFee()`. Copying Shipment's formula means every future price change has to be made twice, and this copy already missed one.

checks.title: label() calls the parent's label()
checks.message: Write `super.label()` to get Shipment's text. Without `super`, `label()` means this same method, so it calls itself until the program crashes.

hints: Both overrides need the same move: get the parent's result first, then add the part that is new.
Shipment's fields are private, so you can't rebuild its label yourself. Ask the parent class for it.
The keyword `super`, then a dot, then the method name calls the parent's version of an overridden method.

test_program.expected_output:
Shipment #1001 to Miami, 2.0 kg
Total: $14.0
Shipment #1002 to Denver, 2.0 kg, insured for $500.0
Insurance fee: $10.0
Total: $24.0

test_program.how_to_run: Put `Shipment.java`, `InsuredShipment.java` and `TestShipments.java` in the same folder, then run `javac *.java` and `java TestShipments`. In an IDE, add all of them to one project and run `TestShipments.java`. You don't type anything: the test program supplies the data.

reflection.question: Explain why `return label() + ...` inside `label()` crashes, but `return super.label() + ...` works.
reflection.model_answer: Inside the override, label() refers to the child's own method, so it calls itself endlessly and fills the call stack. super.label() runs Shipment's version, which returns a string and ends.

labs.scenario:

For the holidays, `PromoGiftCard` adds a $10.0 bonus to every load of $50.0 or more. It writes the bonus straight into `balance`, which is public, so a customer who loaded $495.0 ended up with **$505.0** on the card, and the processor declined it at the register.

Hide the balance so no other class can change it directly, and make the promo add its bonus through the same rule every other load follows. When the bonus would break the limit, the customer simply doesn't get it. The test program then prints:

```

Spend $200.0: true, balance $295.0

```

labs.solution_notes: Keeping data private (information hiding) means it can be changed only by the methods you choose and only in ways you control (p. 347), which is how `load()` guarantees the limit. The bonus that would exceed the limit is refused by `load()`; `loadWithBonus()` still reports `true` because the customer's own money was loaded.

objectives: Declare a method `final` so no subclass can override it

labs.scenario:
Pelican Credit Union's `Loan` class prints a legal notice whose wording is set by the compliance office. Marketing wrote `PromoLoan` and overrode the notice with **No fees, ever!**, which is false (late fees apply) and could get the credit union fined.

The promo class also copied the loan category back when it was *Consumer loan*. `Loan` has said *Personal loan* for a year, but promo statements still print the old name.

Make the notice impossible to override, make the promo category build on the parent's, and lock `PromoLoan` so nobody can subclass it to change the promo terms. The test program then prints:

```
Personal loan: 3 years of interest $1800.0
Personal loan (promo): 2 years of interest $300.0
Promo: Fixed rate. Late fee $35.0 after 10 days.
```

The static `PromoLoan.category()` returns `Loan.category()` followed by ` (promo)`, calling the parent's static method by its class name.
`PromoLoan` is a `final` class.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

labs.solution_notes: A subclass cannot override a method declared `final` (p. 350); with `final` on `legalNotice()`, the marketing override no longer compiles, like Figures 9-25 and 9-26 (p. 351), so it has to go. A subclass cannot override a static method either; a static method with the same signature only hides the parent's (p. 348). A static method receives no `this`, so `super.category()` is not allowed (p. 349), but a child can call the parent's nonprivate static method by class name, `Loan.category()`, as Figure 9-21 does with `BaseballPlayer.showOrigins()` (p. 350). That is also why `@Override` must not be placed on the static method. A `final` class cannot be a parent (p. 351); Java's `Math` class is one (p. 352).

objectives: Declare an abstract class that exists only to be extended

labs.scenario:
Harborside Eats delivers by bike and, since last month, by drone. Every receipt calls `fee()`. To make the code compile, `Delivery` was given a placeholder `fee()` that returns 0.0.

The drone team wrote their pricing, but every drone receipt says **fee $0.0**: their method takes a `double` parameter, so it never replaced the placeholder. Two weeks of drone orders went out free before accounting noticed. No error, no warning.

`BikeDelivery.java` is read-only. Make `Delivery` abstract with an abstract `fee()`, so a missing or misspelled fee becomes a compile error, then fix the drone class. The test program then prints:

```
Order A-105: 4.0 km, fee $11.0
Order A-106: 8.0 km, fee $16.0
```

labs.solution_notes: A class you create only to extend is an abstract class, declared with `abstract`; no objects of it can be created (p. 352). An abstract method has the keyword `abstract`, a header and a semicolon, with no braces and no statements (p. 353), and a concrete subclass must implement every inherited abstract method (p. 353). With the placeholder gone, the starter's `DroneDelivery` doesn't compile, because `fee(double)` overloads instead of overriding: “Don't mistakenly overload an abstract method instead of overriding it” (p. 381). An abstract class may still have fields, a constructor and ordinary methods such as `receipt()`, like the abstract `Vehicle` in the You Do It section (pp. 355–356). When `receipt()` calls `fee()`, the subclass's version runs, the same idea as `speak()` in Figure 9-33 (p. 354).

labs.title: The conference that printed two badges for Priya
labs.subtitle: Override toString(), equals(Object) and hashCode() from the Object class
objectives: Override `toString()` so an object prints useful information
Tell an overloaded `equals(Attendee)` apart from an overriding `equals(Object)`, and write the override safely
Override `hashCode()` so equal objects have equal hash codes
labs.scenario:
At the Gulf Coast Dev Conference, Priya Nair registered twice, once as *priya.nair@example.com* and once as *Priya.Nair@Example.com*. `Attendee` has an `equals()` that compares emails ignoring case, and it says the two registrations are the same person. Yet the check-in desk let her in twice and printed two badges.

The desk is shared with the parking app, so `CheckInDesk` (read-only) stores `Object` references and compares them with `equals(Object)`. The attendee log is no help either: every line reads like **Attendee@1b6d3586**.

Make `Attendee` print as `Name <email>`, override `equals()` so the desk uses it (and so a parking pass or `null` is never “equal” to an attendee), and keep `hashCode()` consistent with it. The test program then prints:

```
Priya Nair <priya.nair@example.com>
Same person? true
Check in Priya: true
Check in Priya again: false
Check in Sam: true
Check in parking pass P-17: true
Entries at the desk: 3
Equal hash codes? true
Equal to null? false
```

requirements.text: `Attendee` overrides `toString()`, marked `@Override`, returning the name, a space and the email in angle brackets.
`Attendee` overrides `equals(Object)` (and no longer has `equals(Attendee)`): it returns `false` for `null` or an object of another class, and otherwise compares emails ignoring case.
`Attendee` overrides `hashCode()` using the email, so two attendees that are equal have the same hash code.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

CheckInDesk.java

labs.solution_notes: Every class extends `Object` and inherits `toString()`, `equals()` and `hashCode()` (p. 364). The inherited `toString()` prints the class name, @ and a hash code (p. 365), so overriding it makes logs readable (pp. 365–366). `equals(Attendee)` has a different parameter list from `Object.equals(Object)`, so it overloads rather than overrides (p. 369); the desk calls `equals(Object)` and gets Object's version, which is true only for the same object (p. 367). The override follows the recommendations on pp. 369–370: true for the same object, false for `null` or a different class, cast only after those tests. Note that each early case must return before the cast: in Figure 9-54 as printed, an argument of another class still reaches the cast. Equal objects should have equal hash codes (p. 370); because `equals()` ignores case, `hashCode()` uses the lowercase email. `a instanceof Attendee` is an accepted alternative to the `getClass()` test.

warmup.question: `priya.equals(priyaAgain)` is true with the starter, yet the desk admits Priya twice. Which `equals()` does the desk's `arrived[x].equals(visitor)` call, and why?
warmup.model_answer: It calls Object's equals(Object), because visitor is an Object reference and Attendee only has an overload that takes an Attendee. Object's version is true only for the very same object, so two registrations are never equal.

warmup.question: What should `equals()` return when an attendee is compared with the String "P-17", and what goes wrong if the method casts the argument to Attendee straight away?
warmup.model_answer: It should return false. Casting a String to Attendee throws a ClassCastException, so the class must be checked before the cast.

checks.message: Add `@Override public int hashCode()` that returns `email.toLowerCase().hashCode()`. Equal attendees must produce equal hash codes, and equals() ignores case, so the hash must too.

reflection.question: The starter's `equals(Attendee)` worked when you called it yourself but not at the desk. Explain the difference between overloading and overriding `equals()` using this bug.
reflection.model_answer: The overload is only chosen when the argument's declared type is Attendee. The desk passes an Object, so Java uses Object's equals(Object). Only an override with the Object parameter replaces the version the desk calls.

reflection.question: Why must `hashCode()` change whenever `equals()` changes? What could go wrong if it didn't?
reflection.model_answer: Equal objects must have equal hash codes. Hash-based collections look an object up by its hash code first, so two equal attendees with different hash codes could both be stored, giving duplicate badges again.

labs.extension: Replace `CheckInDesk`'s array with a `java.util.HashSet<Object>` and its `add()` method, which returns false for a duplicate. Run the test with and without your `hashCode()`: what changes, and why?
labs.worth_knowing: `HashSet` and `HashMap` find an object by its hash code first and only then call `equals()`. If two equal objects have different hash codes, a `HashSet` can store both “duplicates”. That is why Java's documentation requires equal objects to return equal hash codes.

labs.title: The e-bike that couldn't be rented
labs.subtitle: A class has one superclass but can implement any number of interfaces
objectives: Explain why Java doesn't allow a class to extend two classes
Write an interface with abstract methods and a constant, and implement it with `implements`
Write a class header that both extends a class and implements an interface
labs.scenario:
Keys Rentals rents kayaks and, starting this season, electric bikes. The counter software prices anything that is `Rentable`. `Rentable` was written as an abstract class, which worked for `Kayak`, but `ElectricBike` already extends `Bicycle` to share the shop's bike code, and Java won't let it extend `Rentable` as well. So the counter can't quote a price for an e-bike at all.

`Rentable` holds no data except a shared late fee, and no method bodies. That makes it a description of what a rentable item can do, which is exactly what an interface is.

`Bicycle.java` and `RentalCounter.java` are read-only. Turn `Rentable` into an interface and make both items rentable. The test program then prints:

```
Kayak, 14 ft: 3 days $105.0
E-bike, 54 cm frame, 60 km range: 3 days $84.0
E-bike back 2 days late: $94.0
Is a Bicycle: true, is Rentable: true
```

requirements.text: `Rentable` is an `interface` that keeps the `LATE_FEE_PER_DAY` constant and the `dailyRate()` and `rentalTag()` methods.
`Kayak` implements `Rentable` and extends nothing.
`ElectricBike` extends `Bicycle` and implements `Rentable`, and its `rentalTag()` returns, for example, `E-bike, 54 cm frame, 60 km range` from its frame size and range.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects.

Kayak.java

labs.solution_notes: Java prohibits multiple inheritance: a class can't extend two classes (p. 371). An interface is the alternative: its methods are implicitly public and abstract and its data is implicitly public, static and final (p. 371), so the keywords in `Rentable` may be written or left out. A class uses it with `implements`, and must implement every method (p. 371). `ElectricBike extends Bicycle implements Rentable` follows the convention that `implements` comes after `extends` (p. 372), like `WorkingDog extends Dog implements Worker`. An interface constant is shared by every class that uses it without being redeclared (pp. 374–375), so `RentalCounter` reads `Rentable.LATE_FEE_PER_DAY`. Rentable has no data or method bodies to inherit, which fits the advice on p. 374 for choosing an interface over an abstract class. An array of interface references, `Rentable[]`, can hold any implementing objects.

warmup.question: Why can't the starter's ElectricBike be written as `extends Bicycle, Rentable` or given a second `extends`?
warmup.model_answer: Java allows only one superclass per class. ElectricBike already extends Bicycle, so it can't also extend the abstract class Rentable.

warmup.question: Read the starter's `Rentable`. What does it contain that a subclass could inherit and reuse, besides the constant?
warmup.model_answer: Nothing: both methods are abstract and there are no fields or method bodies. It only lists what a rentable item must be able to do, so it might as well be an interface.

The frame size is private in Bicycle, so the tag gets it with `getFrameCm()`; the range is ElectricBike's own field.

reflection.question: Why is an interface the right choice for Rentable here, while Bicycle stays a class?
reflection.model_answer: Rentable only states which methods a rentable item must have and shares a constant, and unrelated items (kayaks, e-bikes) need it alongside their own superclass. Bicycle has real data and behaviour that subclasses reuse, so it stays a class.

labs.worth_knowing: The rule that every interface method is abstract describes interfaces as the book presents them. Since Java 8, an interface may also contain `default` methods with bodies. That is how Java added `forEach()` to its existing collection interfaces without breaking the thousands of classes that already implemented them.

labs.title: The beach heat alert that waits for 35 degrees
labs.subtitle: A record for fixed data, an anonymous inner class and a lambda for one-off rules
objectives: Replace a data-only class with a `record` and use its generated accessors, `equals()` and `toString()`
Implement an interface with an anonymous inner class that uses an effectively final variable
Implement a functional interface with a lambda expression
labs.scenario:
The county's coastal sensors send readings to `Monitor`, which counts how many trigger an alert. Three things are wrong:

- `Reading` is a hand-written class that only holds a station name and a temperature, yet it prints as `Reading@...` and two identical readings are not `equals()`.
- `heatRule(limit)` was supposed to use each station's limit. It returns a `HeatRule` written for one inland station that always uses 35.0, so the beach never alerts at 32.0.
- `freezeRule()` returns `null`, and the program crashes the first time it is counted.

`Rule.java` is read-only: an interface with one method. Make `Reading` a record, write the heat rule as an anonymous inner class and the freeze rule as a lambda. The test program then prints:

```
First reading: Reading[station=Pier 3, celsius=33.5]
Same values, same reading? true
At or above 32.0 C: 2
At or above 35.0 C: 1
Below freezing: 1
Dunes low: -1.5 C at Dunes
```

requirements.text: `Reading` is a `record` with the components `String station` and `double celsius`.
`heatRule(limit)` returns an anonymous inner class that implements `Rule` and triggers when the reading is at or above `limit`; the `HeatRule` class is removed.
`freezeRule()` returns a lambda expression that triggers when the reading is below 0.0.
Running the test program prints exactly what it expects (records need Java 16 or later).

labs.solution_notes: A record (Java 16 and later) declares a class that only holds unchanging data: you list the components and Java generates private final fields, a public constructor, an accessor named after each component (no `get` prefix), and `equals()`, `hashCode()` and `toString()` (pp. 378–379). That is why `today[0]` now prints its values and two readings with the same values are equal. An anonymous inner class is created and instantiated in one `new` expression, implements the interface without the word `implements`, and must end with a semicolon (pp. 379–380). It may use `limit` because the parameter is effectively final: assigned once (p. 380). `Rule` has one abstract method, so it is a functional interface and a lambda can implement it: `r -> r.celsius() < 0.0` (p. 380). A one-line body needs no braces (p. 380). Reading 0.0 is not below freezing, so the freeze count is 1.

warmup.model_answer: It counts 1 (only 36.0). HeatRule ignores the limit parameter and always compares with 35.0, so 33.5 never triggers.

warmup.question: Rule has exactly one abstract method. Why does that matter for writing `freezeRule()`?
warmup.model_answer: An interface with one abstract method is a functional interface, so a lambda expression can implement it; Java knows the lambda is the body of triggers().
